AFEM: Emerging market companies chosen with an active factor approach, tilting toward technology at over two-fifths of the fund, mostly Asian chipmakers and internet firms. It aims to beat plain developing-market index funds by emphasizing the traits its managers believe drive returns there.
AIMS: Small US companies picked by active managers, spread across industrial, technology, health care and financial firms with no single holding dominating. Small caps offer more room to grow and more risk, and this fund's stock selection aims to find the durable growers among thousands of small names.
ALTL: Large US stocks in an alternator design: the fund switches between a defensive low-volatility lineup and a higher-octane one, following a rules-based risk signal from Lunt Capital. When the signal says risk on it chases growth names; when it says risk off it hides in steadier industries like utilities.
ARP: A risk parity approach that balances stocks, bonds, commodities and gold so each contributes similar risk, then adapts the mix to broad economic trends. Right now commodities carry the largest weight, and the balancing act aims for steadier results across booms and busts alike.
BKSE: Six hundred small US companies spread across every industry, technology, finance, industry and consumer firms in small slices each. It is a core small cap holding that owns the whole small-company market rather than picking winners, accepting the group's bigger swings in exchange for its growth potential.
CVSM: Small and mid-sized US companies picked by active managers, spread across finance, consumer, industrial and drug firms rather than concentrated in technology. It hunts for growth in the market's middle ranks, where companies are big enough to be proven but small enough to still expand quickly.
DDTL: Built to gain from moves in either direction over its one-year July period: it can profit when large US stocks fall moderately as well as when they rise, up to a cap. The 10 in its name is the buffer meant to absorb deeper losses first.
DISK: Memory chip companies: the makers of the DRAM, flash and storage chips that computers and AI data centers remember with, mostly in Korea, Japan and the US. Three Asian giants are about half the fund, so it is a concentrated bet on the memory cycle's booms and busts.
DOGG: The ten highest-yielding stocks in the Dow Jones Industrial Average, the classic Dogs of the Dow list, paired with Treasuries and options to target income well above the Dow's own dividend yield. It is a concentrated income bet on ten blue-chip payers at a time.
DYNB: A flexible bond portfolio that moves between investment grade debt and junk bonds as its managers see opportunity, currently leaning heavily on US Treasuries. It is built for income with freedom to roam, so its riskiness rises and falls with how boldly the managers reach for yield.
EGGQ: Fast-growing technology stocks, data storage, optical networking and AI power equipment, paired with an options portfolio that sells contracts against the positions for income. It aims to blend growth with a payout stream, and the options can trim gains when its high-flying holdings jump.
EXPN: Large US companies its managers see as expansion leaders, technology at nearly half, plus an occasional options overlay for commodity-linked returns. The commodity twist sets it apart from plain growth funds, adding an extra engine that can help or hurt depending on raw material prices.
FLCE: A curated bundle of large-cap stock funds from big-name managers, mixing growth, value, dividend and factor approaches in one holding. Frontier assembles and rebalances the manager mix, so it is a fund of funds for investors who want active stock management without choosing managers themselves.
FTCE: One hundred US companies with the highest earnings quality in their sectors, chosen by forensic accounting research that checks whether reported profits are backed by real cash. Technology leads at about two-fifths, and the earnings capture screen sets it apart from plain index funds.
GLIN: Indian companies scored for growth and quality: the stock exchange itself, telecoms, retailers, defense and cable makers, with banks and finance at over a third. It is a single-country growth bet that favors fundamental strength over simply owning India's biggest names.
HBDC: Bonds issued by business development companies, the publicly traded lenders that finance mid-sized private businesses, all in one fund. It pays corporate-bond-like income with a twist: the borrowers are themselves lenders, so their health rises and falls with the private credit market.
HBR: A single cryptocurrency, HBAR, the token of the Hedera network, held directly as the trust's only digital asset. It gives brokerage-account exposure to a coin built for fast, cheap transactions, and like all single-coin funds it can swing violently with crypto sentiment.
HIS: A focused portfolio of large US companies, technology at over two-fifths, chosen by its managers rather than copied from an index. It works as an active core stock holding, so its results depend on a select set of picks and can differ noticeably from the broad market.
IBIH: Inflation-protected US Treasury bonds, called TIPS, all maturing in 2031, whose principal rises with inflation. Because every bond matures the same year, it works like buying one inflation-proof bond: hold to 2031 and the inflation adjustment is locked in, while prices swing before then.
IQM: Companies building intelligent machines: the chips, networking gear, testing equipment and power systems behind artificial intelligence and automation, with technology nearly three-quarters of the fund. It is a growth bet on the machinery of the AI era rather than on any single application.
IWMY: An options strategy on small US companies designed to pay distributions every week, using the Russell 2000 group of smaller stocks as its engine. Weekly payouts are the point, and gains are capped, so it is an income tool built on a volatile corner of the market.
JPY: Japanese companies picked by Lazard's managers, who rotate toward whichever industries look strongest at each stage of the economic cycle. Banks, chip equipment, electronics and trading firms all feature, giving actively managed Japan exposure rather than a plain slice of its market.
MARW: Options on large US stocks across every major industry, arranged to absorb the first 20 percent of losses over a one-year period running from March to February. In exchange for that deep buffer it accepts a cap on gains, suiting investors who fear a serious downturn most.
MBSD: Mortgage bonds guaranteed by US agencies like Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, the pooled home loans of American borrowers, managed with tight control over interest rate sensitivity. It aims for steady income a step above Treasuries, with its disciplined duration keeping price swings in check.
MILN: Companies selling to millennial consumers, the generation born between 1980 and 2000: phones, online shopping, travel stays, food delivery, sneakers and streaming. Consumer brands are over half the fund, making it a bet on one generation's spending habits as it reaches peak earning years.
MMCA: California municipal bonds maturing in the intermediate range, from the state's universities, airports, cities and clean energy authorities. Their interest is exempt from both federal and California income tax, a double exemption that sets it apart for California taxpayers in higher brackets.
MSFO: An options strategy built on one stock, Microsoft, selling call options against its price moves to turn them into monthly income. The trade-off is capped gains when the stock jumps, and income that rises and falls with how jumpy the market expects Microsoft to be.
MSTW: An options and swap strategy built on one very volatile stock, MicroStrategy, the software company famous for holding bitcoin, designed to pay income weekly. Weekly payouts from such a jumpy stock can be large, but the same swings that create the income can slash the fund's value.
NFEB: Options on the Nasdaq-100, the big technology and internet companies, with a power buffer that absorbs a first slice of losses over a one-year period resetting each February. It is built for investors who want growth-stock exposure with a shock absorber, accepting capped gains in return.
NSEP: Options on the Nasdaq-100, the big technology and internet companies, with a power buffer that absorbs a first slice of losses over a one-year period resetting each September. It is built for investors who want growth-stock exposure with a shock absorber, accepting capped gains in return.
NUMI: Municipal bonds from across the US, toll roads, schools, universities and towns, actively chosen for tax-exempt income. The interest escapes federal income tax, which sets it apart from taxable bond funds and makes it a staple for higher earners investing outside retirement accounts.
OAKI: Large companies outside the US bought when their prices look depressed, from European banks and sportswear brands to caterers and hotels. Oakmark's managers are patient contrarians, so it is a value fund that often buys what others are avoiding and holds for years.
PBJ: US food and beverage companies: soda and energy drink giants, coffee chains, snack and chocolate makers, grocery stores and farm suppliers. Food is a classic defensive industry, since people eat in good times and bad, so the fund tends to swing less than the broad market.
PFOE: Fifteen to thirty companies worldwide that its managers judge to be high-quality growers, from music and streaming platforms to chip equipment and health insurers. Such a short list makes it a conviction portfolio: each pick counts, for better or worse.
PGJ: Chinese companies listed on US exchanges: online shopping, gaming, search, restaurants and delivery platforms headquartered in China but traded in New York. It is a bet on China's consumer internet through American-listed shares, carrying both China policy risk and US listing risk.
PTBD: A trend-following bond strategy that switches between high yield corporate bonds and intermediate Treasuries, fully in one, half and half, or fully defensive, depending on which way bond markets are trending. The rule-based switching aims to ride good times and sidestep credit downturns.
QABA: Community banks: the small and mid-sized local lenders listed on US exchanges, from regional banking groups to hometown institutions. It is a pure bet on Main Street banking, so it moves with local economies, loan demand and interest rates rather than with the giant money-center banks.
QXQ: Nasdaq-100 companies, the big technology and internet names, paired with an actively traded options strategy that sells contracts to generate current income. It aims to pay more than the growth index yields on its own, giving up some upside when tech stocks surge.
RDFI: Closed-end bond funds bought for their income, many trading at discounts to the assets they hold, with a heavy lean toward emerging market debt funds. Buying discounted funds can add extra yield, though the discounts and the underlying loans add layers of risk and complexity.
RSJN: Options on an equal-weight basket of large US stocks, where every company counts the same, with a cushion that absorbs a first slice of losses over a one-year period resetting each June. Equal weighting shrinks the tech giants' dominance compared with ordinary large-cap funds.
RSPR: Every real estate company in a major US large-cap index, held in equal weights: senior housing, malls, offices, hotels and data centers alike. Equal weighting keeps the giants from dominating, giving smaller landlords the same say as the biggest property owners.
SOCL: Social media companies worldwide: the platforms behind messaging, short video, social networking and online communities in the US, China and Korea. It is a focused bet on the attention economy, and these firms swing with advertising spending, regulation and user growth headlines.
SOVF: Mid-sized US companies picked by active managers, leaning toward technology and payment firms alongside health care and industrial names. It is a stock picker's mid-cap fund, aiming to catch companies in the sweet spot between small and large, with the growth potential and volatility that implies.
SPXE: Large US companies across every major industry except one: energy is left out entirely, so there are no oil, gas or pipeline firms. It suits investors avoiding fossil fuel stocks without hand-picking, though it will lag whenever energy shares lead the market.
STBF: Short-term bonds actively traded across the quality spectrum, from Treasuries to below-investment-grade debt, all maturing soon. Short maturities keep its price calm when interest rates move, and active allocation lets the managers hunt for extra yield without taking long-term rate risk.
THY: A tactical income fund that shifts among high yield bonds, investment grade bonds, municipals, Treasuries and cash, and can hedge or retreat entirely to cash when its managers judge risk too high. That freedom sets it apart: safety, not yield, takes over in stormy markets.
TSEL: Select US growth companies hand-picked by Sands Capital, with technology over half the fund, from chipmakers to specialty steel and power infrastructure firms. Sands holds a focused list of businesses it believes can compound earnings for years, accepting concentration as the price of conviction.
VAMO: US stocks that are both cheap and trending upward, currently heavy in energy refiners and financial firms, with the ability to hedge the whole portfolio when trends break down. That hedge, which can leave it holding mostly cash, sets it apart from always-invested value funds.
WRTH: An options income strategy guided by chart analysis, reading price patterns to decide where to sell contracts, with Treasury bills held as collateral. The chart-driven approach sets it apart from systematic covered call funds: trades follow a technician's view of the market's direction.
XB: Corporate bonds rated B, a single slice of the junk bond market below the stronger BB tier and above the riskiest CCC names. It pays higher interest than safer high yield funds in exchange for borrowers with shakier finances, so defaults are the ever-present trade-off.
